newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX oil prices end firm on bargain hunting.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX oil prices end firm on bargain hunting.

text.p: NYMEX oil prices ended on a firm note Thursday as traders went bargain hunting following a sell-off Wednesday due to to increasing crude supplies.
"We had been oversold after the market weakened on high imports. By the end of April, we could see better gasoline demand," said Mike De Luca, trader with Prudential Securities.
May gasoline ended 0.29 cent higher at 60.90 cents a gallon. May heating oil settled 0.74 cent a gallon up at 53.26 cents while May crude ended unchanged at $19.47 a barrel.

"I am still looking for a gasoline rally even though funds have been disappointed after trying to get into the rally early," said William Brown, president of trading firm W.H. Brown & Co. Gasoline typically rallies in the spring in anticipation of the summer driving season.
Gasoline was helped in part by a delayed restart of a 64,000 barrel per day (bpd) gasoline making machine at Phillips Petroleum Co's 185,000 bpd refinery in Sweeny, Texas.
Phillips would not say why the restart was delayed at the unit which had been shut for over a month for maintenance, although it hoped to restart the unit by this evening.
Earlier in the session, May gasoline fell as low as 60.15 cents but found technical support near 60.00 cents, spot gasoline's lowest point since February 24.

Although prompt crude resisted losses, it rose as much as 32 cents to $19.79 before giving up its gains and widening its contango to June. Contango indicates the current contract is cheaper than the later contract.
The May/June spread ended with a 10 cent contango versus seven cents Wednesday.
Over the past week, May gasoline has fallen more than four cents a gallon while May crude has fallen $1.37 a barrel. Spot crude is trading at its lowest level since March 1996.

Oil inventory data for the week ended March 28 by the American Petroleum Institute (API) Tuesday said crude imports rose sharply to 7.7 million bpd from 6.8 million bpd due to an influx of West African crude.
The data also reflected lacklustre implied gasoline demand of 7.4 million barrels per day.

But, the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA) said Thursday that U.S. gasoline demand this summer is expected to rise to a record 8.14 million barrels per day, up 1.8 percent from last summer.
-- Harry Milling, New York Energy Desk, 212-859-1761
